name: Uma Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for letting me come up, Uma. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at five, kettle on, and out to the ewes before the light. Rui and I farm Costa Hill, three hundred hectares of hill ground: six hundred ewes, eighty suckler cows, hay off the low fields and a bit of barley. My great-grandfather cleared the top field with a horse and his own back. In lambing I'm in the shed half the night, and the rest of the year it's checking stock on the quad bike, fencing, and keeping two hired men and my son busy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a good ewe lamb. I judge at the county show, and our Texel crosses have taken the breed championship four times. What wears me out is forms and people telling me how to farm from an office. I don't have one of those smartphones and I've never used AI. If I need something off the computer, Maria, my daughter, does it for me on a Sunday after church.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about your family and life around the farm.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rui's sixty-one and his hip's going, so I run the farm day to day now. João, our son, is an electrician but he works with us at weekends, and the plan's always been that he takes over. Maria's married with three little ones down in the village. We're fine for money: no debt, land's ours, and we've savings. I'm fifty-eight, and I've no intention of stopping while I can still lift a ewe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's the one I'd pick, if anybody asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be like that. People in cities get excited about every new gadget and then it fizzles out. At the show or after church I'd say it with a smile, because I'd be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I'd say. It means Costa Hill stays as it is and João takes it on as planned. Maybe Maria fills the forms in faster on a Sunday, and that's no harm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Same flock, same men, same lambing. We'd keep putting a bit by each year, the way we always have, and I'd carry on judging at the show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the morning after the last ewe has lambed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said city people get excited about every gadget. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young chap from the supermarket's buying team, mostly. He came up with a tablet and asked about our carbon score. Lovely lad, never seen a lamb born. Those are the people who'd have been disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would João be disappointed, being a younger man?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might, a bit. He likes his gadgets, being an electrician. But he'd be glad the farm was safe. He knows what it means to us.

S0.say: I'd say it was always going to fizzle out, like every gadget city people get excited about. I'd say it with a smile after church, because I'd be glad.
S0.think: It means the farm stays as it is and my son takes it on as planned. My daughter might do the forms faster on a Sunday, which is no harm.
S0.do: Changes nothing: same flock, same hired men, same lambing. Keeps saving a bit each year and keeps judging at the county show.
S0.feel: Calm, like the morning after the last ewe has lambed.
S0.quote: Lovely lad, never seen a lamb born.
S0.fieldNote: Uma ties her identity to four generations on the land and to winning at the county show. She uses no technology herself and relies on her daughter for computer tasks. A plateau confirms her view of city enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's the one the farming papers keep pushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good farmers will still be needed, whatever the machines do. I'd say that at the show, and I'd mean it about stockmanship. I'd say young people should learn a proper trade through an apprenticeship, not sit in front of a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the neighbours. The Pereiras below us are already struggling, and if the big farms get robots and cheaper lamb, they'll sell up. Then the valley changes, and the chapel loses another family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as we are, but I'd keep a closer eye on the money and not buy the new tractor this year. I wouldn't buy any of the robots. If João wanted to try something, I'd let him do it on his own time, on his own small patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing dark clouds over the next valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the Pereiras sold up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the free market, the market's fair if everyone plays straight. I'd blame the big companies that own the machines and the supermarkets both. They squeeze from both ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let João try something on his own patch. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's been on at me about drones for checking the hill. I'd say fine, take the top field, and if a drone can find a cast ewe faster than my dog, I'll eat my hat. I don't think I'll be eating any hats.

S1.say: I'd say good farmers will still be needed whatever the machines do, and young people should learn a proper trade through apprenticeships, not sit in front of screens.
S1.think: I'd worry for neighbours who are already struggling and would sell if big farms get robots and cheaper lamb. Then the valley changes and the chapel loses another family.
S1.do: Carries on but watches money more closely and postpones a new tractor. Buys no robots herself, but lets her son try drones on one field in his own time.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like dark clouds over the next valley.
S1.quote: If a drone can find a cast ewe faster than my dog, I'll eat my hat.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is for the valley community and the chapel, not her own finances. She defends the free market but blames big companies that own both machines and supermarkets. She gives her son a small, fenced-off space to experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That can't be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody stops to think. After church I'd say we need to look after our own: family, neighbours, the parish. I wouldn't be asking the government for handouts, but I'd say they've a duty to stop this happening so fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it frightens me. Not the money, we've land and savings. It's that João wouldn't take on a farm that a robot can run better than him, and why would he? Four generations, and it ends with me watching a machine on the top field from the kitchen window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd dig in. Same flock, same men, for as long as anyone buys our lambs. I'd put more by, maybe stop the holiday we take after shearing, and sit down with Rui, João and Maria in the first week to talk about the farm. And I'd lean on the chapel and the neighbours, because that's what they're for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep, I know that. Like the year of foot-and-mouth, when every lorry on the road could've been the one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years' warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no time for João to make his own choice. With more time he could try it, fail or not, and decide. With two years, the decision's made for him by people we'll never meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd dig in. If the price of lamb fell because of the robots, how long could you keep going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Years, if I'm honest about the savings. We could farm at a loss for a long time. But I'm not sure I'd want to be the last woman in the valley lambing by hand, just to prove something. I don't know. I'd have to pray on that.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when nobody stops to think. We must look after our own family, neighbours and parish, and the government has a duty to stop it moving so fast, without handouts.
S2.think: It frightens me, not for money but because my son wouldn't take on a farm a robot runs better than him. Four generations would end with me watching a machine from the kitchen window.
S2.do: Digs in with the same flock and staff for as long as lambs sell. Saves more and drops the after-shearing holiday, calls a family meeting in the first week and leans on the chapel and neighbours.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, like the year of foot-and-mouth disease.
S2.quote: Four generations, and it ends with me watching a machine on the top field from the kitchen window.
S2.fieldNote: Uma's alarm is about the end of a family line on the land, not money; she could farm at a loss for years. Two years takes away her son's chance to choose for himself. She'd turn to family, faith and neighbours rather than the state, while still saying government has a duty to slow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast. I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've a few years, so let's use them to teach the young ones the old skills while there's time. I'd want the breed society to run apprenticeships, so lambing and stockmanship aren't lost. Somebody has to know how to do it if the machines break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives João time, which is what I'd want for him. He could try the farm with whatever machines come, or go back to being an electrician, and choose properly. It still hurts, but it's not being pushed off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand João more of the decisions straight away, starting with the cattle. I'd keep lambing the way we do, and I'd take on a young lad from the village as an apprentice, so the skills go somewhere. I'd keep saving and not spend on anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like a long illness in the family: you know it's coming, and you try to make the time count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give João a real choice and give me time to show him everything. Two years, I'd be fighting. Five, I'd be teaching. Teaching's better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the new machines yourself, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's not stubbornness, it's knowing myself. João can have them. I'll stay in the lambing shed, and the machine can stay out of it while I'm there.

S3.say: I'd say we should use the years to teach young people the old skills, with breed society apprenticeships in lambing and stockmanship, so someone knows how if the machines break.
S3.think: It gives my son time to try the farm with machines or return to his trade, and to choose properly. It still hurts, but it's not being pushed off a cliff.
S3.do: Hands her son more decisions straight away, starting with the cattle. Keeps lambing as now, takes on a village apprentice to pass the skills on and keeps saving without new spending.
S3.feel: Anxious, like a long illness in the family when she tries to make the time count.
S3.quote: Two years, I'd be fighting. Five, I'd be teaching. Teaching's better.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years turn her from fighting to passing things on. She still won't use machines herself but wants skills preserved through apprenticeships, in line with her views. The emotional weight is in succession, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight. Still lambing, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families to decide properly. I'd tell people at the show that the farms that last will be the ones where the family stays together and passes things on. Ten years is long enough for that, if you start talking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's easier, but it doesn't really go away. João would have time to make the farm his own, with or without the machines, and I'd step back slowly. I'd still be sad that the grandchildren might never lamb a ewe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and slowly hand over to João over five or six years. I'd teach Maria's eldest at lambing, he's nine, so he knows what it is even if he never does it for a living. I wouldn't buy machines, but I wouldn't stop João.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more at peace. Like knowing winter's coming in October rather than in a sudden snow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the grandchildren might never lamb a ewe. Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than anything else in this conversation. It's not about money or work. It's about knowing where your food comes from, and that you can bring a life into the world with your own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to the government, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say leave families alone to work it out, and keep the apprenticeships going. Don't send us cheques, help us train our own. That's all I'd ask.

S4.say: I'd say there's time for families to decide properly, and the farms that last will be those where the family stays together and passes things on.
S4.think: It's easier but doesn't go away. My son would have time to make the farm his own and I'd step back slowly, but I'd still be sad the grandchildren might never lamb a ewe.
S4.do: Carries on and hands over to her son over five or six years. Teaches her nine-year-old grandson at lambing and leaves machines to her son without buying any herself.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more at peace, like winter announced in October rather than a sudden snow.
S4.quote: It's about knowing where your food comes from, and that you can bring a life into the world with your own hands.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years removes the panic but not the grief about skills dying out. She asks government for apprenticeships rather than cheques, consistent with her views. Teaching her grandson is her way of keeping the knowledge alive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It takes away the time to hand over properly. What would help is apprenticeships for farm skills, paid for properly, and rules that stop the big companies owning everything at once. Not money in the post. Just a fair chance for families.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dog. Bess has worked this hill nine years. Whatever comes, I'll not be swapping her for a drone, and I'd like that written down somewhere.

headlineQuote: Whatever comes, I'll not be swapping her for a drone, and I'd like that written down somewhere.
portrait: Uma Costa, 58, runs Costa Hill, a fourth-generation hill farm with 600 ewes and 80 suckler cows, alongside her husband Rui, two hired men and her electrician son João, who is meant to take over. She judges sheep at the county show, has never used AI, and relies on her daughter for anything on a computer. She is financially secure, so her fears are about the family line, the valley community and skills dying out. She is calm in the plateau picture, uneasy as neighbours come under pressure, and alarmed by AGI in two years because her son would lose the chance to choose. With more time she moves from fighting to teaching, preferring apprenticeships and family over government money.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would take away the time to hand the farm over properly to her son.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid apprenticeships for farm skills and rules stopping big companies from owning everything, not money in the post.
